title: Judging liveability with geographical concepts

match.reason: No bank point teaches the three concepts of space, environment and interconnection for judging liveability; the closest, Interconnection, covers only one of the three and the others cover different ideas such as measuring liveability or strategies.

draft.title: Judging liveability with geographical concepts
card: Geographers use geographical concepts to judge how liveable a place is. This gives them a clear way to look at a place, instead of just giving an opinion.
where things are located and how easy they are to reach, such as schools, clinics, shops and parks.
the quality of the surroundings, such as clean air and water, green space and the risk of floods or fires.
the links a place has to people, jobs and other places, such as roads, trains and internet access.
draft.remember: Ask where services are, how good the surroundings are, and how well the place is linked to others.

a.q: A geographer checks how far residents of a suburb live from the nearest hospital and school. Which concept is being used?
a.why: The geographer is looking at where services are and how easy they are to reach, which is space. Interconnection is about links to people, jobs and other places, not about the location of services.
a.clue: Think about where things are located.

b.q: A town in country Victoria has clean air and a large park. Its train line was closed, so many people cannot easily reach jobs in the city. Which concept shows the town's weakness?
opts: Interconnection, because links to jobs are poor
Environment, because the surroundings are poor
Space, because the town has too few parks
Environment, because the train line closed
b.why: Poor links to jobs in the city are a problem of interconnection. The town's environment is a strength, as it has clean air and a large park, so it is not the weakness here.
b.clue: The air and the park are good. What is the problem about?

b.best: Interconnection, because links to jobs are poor
